questions.question: Let WB and WT be two set associative cache organizations that use LRU algorithm for cache block replacement. WB is a write back cache and WT is a write through cache. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: Each cache block in WB and WT has a dirty bit.
options.B: Every write hit in WB leads to a data transfer from cache to main memory.
options.C: Eviction of a block from WT will not lead to data transfer from cache to main memory.
options.D: A read miss in WB will never lead to eviction of a dirty block from WB.

questions.explanation:
Check each statement (we need the FALSE ones):
- "Each block in WB and WT has a dirty bit": WT writes memory on every write, so it needs no dirty bit [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Every write hit in WB transfers data to memory": WB only sets the dirty bit; memory is updated on eviction [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- "Eviction from WT causes no transfer to memory": memory is already up to date [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "A read miss in WB never evicts a dirty block": the LRU victim can be dirty [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 1, 2 and 4

questions.question:

Interrupt from CPU temperature sensor (raises interrupt if CPU temperature is too high)

questions.question:
A 4-way set-associative cache memory unit with a capacity of 16 KB is built using a block
size of 8 words. The word length is 32 bits. The size of the physical address space is 4 GB.
The number of bits for the TAG field is _____
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Block = 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 B = 32 B [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] offset = 5 bits
- Blocks = 16 KB / 32 B = 512, sets = 512 / 4 = 128 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] index = 7 bits
- Address = 4 GB [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 32 bits

TAG = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 7 [latex]-[/latex] 5 = 20 bits

Answer: 20

questions.question: A processor has 40 distinct instructions and 24 general purpose registers. A 32-bit instruction word has an opcode, two register operands and an immediate operand. The number of bits available for the immediate operand field is _______ .

- 40 instructions [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] opcode [latex]\lceil\log_2 40\rceil=6[/latex] bits
- 24 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 bits each, two operands = 10 bits

Immediate = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 6 [latex]-[/latex] 10 = 16 bits

Answer: 16

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.

I. Daisy chaining is used to assign priorities in attending interrupts.
II. When a device raises a vectored interrupt, the CPU does polling to identify the source of interrupt.
III. In polling,the CPU periodically checks the status bits to know if any device needs its attention.
IV. During DMA, both the CPU and DMA controller can be bus masters at the same time.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- I: daisy chaining serially connects devices; the one nearest the CPU gets highest priority [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- II: a vectored interrupt supplies the ISR address itself, so no polling is needed [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- III: that is the definition of polling [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- IV: only one bus master at a time; the CPU gives up the bus during DMA [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: I and III only

questions.question: A processor has 64 registers and uses 16-bit instruction format. It has two types of instructions: I-type and R-type. Each I-type instruction contains an opcode, a register name, and a 4-bit immediate value. Each R-type instruction contains an opcode and two register names. If there are 8 distinct I-type opcodes, then the maximum number of distinct R-type opcodes is _______.
questions.explanation:
Register field = [latex]\log_2 64=6[/latex] bits.
- I-type: opcode + 6 + 4 = 16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6-bit opcode.
- R-type: opcode + 6 + 6 = 16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4-bit opcode.

Expanding opcodes: one 4-bit R-type code, followed by 2 more bits, gives 4 I-type opcodes. The 8 I-type opcodes need 8/4 = 2 of the 16 four-bit codes.

R-type opcodes = 16 [latex]-[/latex] 2 = 14

Answer: 14

questions.question:
A file system uses an in-memory cache to cache disk blocks.The miss rate of the cache is shown in the figure. The latency to read a block from the cache is 1 ms and to read a block from the disk is 10ms. Assume that the cost of checking whether a block exists in the cache is negligible. Available cache sizes are in multiples of 10MB.

The smallest cache size required to ensure an average read latency of less than 6ms is_________ MB.
questions.explanation:
Average latency = (1 [latex]-[/latex] m) [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + m [latex]\times[/latex] 10 = 1 + 9m (m = miss rate). We need [latex]1+9m \lt 6\Rightarrow m \lt 0.556[/latex].

From the graph: 20 MB gives 60% (too high), 30 MB gives 40% [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] latency 1 + 3.6 = 4.6 ms True

Answer: 30

questions.question:
An application loads 100 libraries at startup. Loading each library requires exactly
one disk access. The seek time of the disk to a random location is given as 10ms.
Rotational speed of disk is 6000rpm. If all 100 libraries are loaded from random
locations on the disk, how long does it take to load all libraries? (The time to
transfer data from the disk block once the head has been positioned at the start
of the block may be neglected)

questions.question:
Consider a RISC machine where each instruction is exactly 4 bytes long. Conditional and unconditional branch instructions use PC- relative addressing mode with Offset specified in bytes to the target location of the branch instruction. Further the Offset is always with respect to the address of the next instruction in the program sequence. Consider the following instruction sequence.

If the target of the branch instruction is i, then the decimal value of the Offset is __________
questions.explanation:
The offset is measured from the instruction after the branch, i.e. i + 4 (in instruction numbers). The target is i, which is 4 instructions back.

Offset = [latex]-[/latex]4 [latex]\times[/latex] 4 bytes = [latex]-[/latex]16

Answer: -16

questions.question: Suppose the functions F and G can be computed in 5 and 3 nano seconds by functional units [latex]U_{F}[/latex] and [latex]U_{G}[/latex], respectively. Given two instances of [latex]U_{F}[/latex] and two instances of [latex]U_{G}[/latex], it is required to implement the computation [latex]F(G(X_{i}))[/latex] for [latex]1\leq i\leq 10[/latex]. Ignoring all other delays, the minimum time required to complete this computation is ________ nanoseconds.
questions.explanation:
Each item needs G (3 ns) then F (5 ns). With 2 units of each, the F units are the bottleneck: 10 F computations on 2 units = 5 rounds [latex]\times[/latex] 5 ns = 25 ns.

F can start only after the first G results are ready (3 ns), and the G units keep feeding F in time after that.

Total = 3 + 25 = 28 ns

Answer: 28

questions.question: An instruction pipeline has five stages, namely, instruction fetch (IF), instruction decode and register fetch (ID/RF), instruction execution (Ex), memory access (MEM), and register write back (WB) with stage latencies 1 ns, 2.2 ns, 2 ns, 1 ns, and 0.75 ns, respectively (ns stands for nanoseconds). To gain in terms of frequency, the designers have decided to split the ID/RF stage into three stages (ID, RF1, RF2) each of latency 2.2/3 ns. Also, the Ex stage is split into two stages (Ex1, Ex2) each of latency 1 ns. The new design has a total of eight pipeline stages. A program has 20% branch instructions which execute in the Ex stage and produce the next instruction pointer at the end of the Ex stage in the old design and at the end of the Ex2 stage in the new design. The IF stage stalls after fetching a branch instruction until the next instruction pointer is computed. All instructions other than the branch instruction have an average CPI of one in both the designs. The execution times of this program on the old and the new design are P and Q nanoseconds, respectively. The value of P/Q is __________
questions.explanation:
Old design: clock = 2.2 ns. Branch resolved at end of stage 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 stall cycles.
CPI = 0.8 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + 0.2 [latex]\times[/latex] 3 = 1.4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P = 1.4 [latex]\times[/latex] 2.2 = 3.08 ns per instruction

New design: clock = 1 ns. Branch resolved at end of Ex2 = stage 6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 5 stall cycles.
CPI = 0.8 [latex]\times[/latex] 1 + 0.2 [latex]\times[/latex] 6 = 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q = 2 ns per instruction

P/Q = 3.08 / 2 = 1.54

Answer: 1.54

questions.question:
Consider two set-associative cache memory architectures: WBC, which uses the
write back policy, and WTC, which uses the write through policy. Both of them use
the LRU (Least Recently Used) block replacement policy. The cache memory is
connected to the main memory. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.A: A read miss in WBC never evicts a dirty block
options.B:
A read miss in WTC never triggers a write back operation of a cache block to
main memory
options.C: A write hit in WBC can modify the value of the dirty bit of a cache block
options.D:
A write miss in WTC always writes the victim cache block to main memory
before loading the missed block to the cache

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- WBC read miss: the LRU victim may be dirty and then it must be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE ("never" is wrong).
- WTC read miss: with write-through, memory is always up to date, so a victim never needs to be written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WBC write hit: the block becomes dirty, so the dirty bit can change from 0 to 1 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- WTC write miss: the victim block is never dirty, so it is never written back [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

questions.question:
A cache memory unit with capacity of N words and block size of B words is to be designed.
If it is designed as a direct mapped cache, the length of the TAG field is 10 bits. If the cache
unit is now designed as a 16-way set-associative cache, the length of the TAG field is
______bits.
questions.explanation:
Direct mapped: N/B lines. 16-way: (N/B)/16 sets, i.e. 16 = [latex]2^4[/latex] times fewer sets [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] the index loses 4 bits, which go to the tag.

Tag = 10 + 4 = 14 bits

Answer: 14

questions.question:
A computer system with a word length of 32 bits has a 16 MB byte- addressable main memory and a 64 KB, 4-way set associative cache memory with a block size of 256 bytes. Consider the following four physical addresses represented in hexadecimal notation.

A1=0x42C8A4,
A2=0x546888,
A3=0x6A289C,
A4=0x5E4880

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: A1 and A4 are mapped to different cache sets.
options.B: A2 and A3 are mapped to the same cache set.
options.C: A3 and A4 are mapped to the same cache set.
options.D: A1 and A3 are mapped to the same cache set.

questions.explanation:
Lines = 64 KB / 256 B = 256; sets = 256 / 4 = 64 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 set bits after the 8 offset bits.
Set = (address / 256) mod 64, i.e. the low 6 bits of the address without its last two hex digits:
- A1 = 0x42C8A4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0x42C8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] set 8
- A2 = 0x546888 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0x5468 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] set 40
- A3 = 0x6A289C [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0x6A28 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] set 40
- A4 = 0x5E4880 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0x5E48 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] set 8

A2 and A3 share set 40 (A1 and A4 share set 8).

Answer: A2 and A3 are mapped to the same cache set
